title: The Right’s Identity Politics Take a Bizarre Turn
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
If you want a snapshot of how the right has changed over the past decade, here’s one data point: MAGA activists think Sarah Huckabee Sanders is too woke now
That’s the same Sarah Huckabee Sanders who is the daughter of the GOP fixture Mike Huckabee and a former White House press secretary for President Trump

Now governor of Arkansas, she’s facing criticism from right-wing influencers over an ad boosting the state’s imposition of work requirements for recipients of the state’s Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act

These requirements are a long-standing Republican priority, but my colleague Annie Lowrey wrote last year that they are “a terrible idea” : The requirement creates new taxpayer costs and red tape without really solving any problem, because most Medicaid recipients who are physically able to work already do
That’s not why the activists are mad, though
They’re upset because the face of loafing in Sanders’s ad is a cheese-ball-snarfing couch potato named Brad who is a young white man
The “Pizzagate” influencer Jack Posobiec labels it “ Antiwhite .” Sean Davis of The Federalist calls it part of decades-long, systematic discrimination against white men

The openly bigoted investor James Fishback , fresh off getting trounced in a GOP primary for governor of Florida, traveled to Little Rock this week to rail against the “ false and disgraceful ad .” Assessing the accuracy of a fictional character in an ad feels a little absurd, but for the record: More than 60 percent of Medicaid-expansion enrollees in Arkansas are white, and 18 percent are Black, according to The New York Times . (The state overall is about 75 percent white and 15 percent Black.) A little more than half are women

Sanders rebuffed criticism, writing , “Next thing you know they’ll say I should have used cookies instead of cheese balls.” The immediate and obsessive focus on a throwaway character in a 30-second ad is a lurid reminder of how identitarianism has become influential in segments of the American right, particularly young voters
This is a matter of how members of the movement understand politics, as well as how they attempt to communicate to the American public
For decades, the right—as well as some centrist Democrats, such as Bill Clinton—criticized progressives for embracing identity politics
They argued that a focus on demographic segments was divisive and unhelpful

Ronald Reagan preached that “a rising tide lifts all boats” (though in practice this often meant support for trickle-down policies that helped mostly the already-thriving) and called for “color-blind” policies (which also tended to result in worse outcomes for people of color)
This impulse persists in some segments of the Republican Party, most notably in the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court, led by the former Reagan aide John Roberts
This didn’t mean that people on the right hesitated to use race as a political wedge
The avatar of this strategy was Lee Atwater, an adviser to Reagan and George H

Bush, whose 1981 explanation was as vulgar as the impulses he courted. “You start out in 1954 by saying, ‘Nigger, nigger, nigger,’” he explained . “By 1968 you can’t say ‘nigger’—that hurts you, backfires
So you say stuff like, uh, ‘forced busing,’ ‘states’ rights,’ and all that stuff, and you’re getting so abstract

Now you’re talking about cutting taxes, and all these things you’re talking about are totally economic things and a by-product of them is, Blacks get hurt worse than whites.” In 1980, for example, Reagan delivered a controversial speech at the Neshoba County Fair in Mississippi, not far from where the civil-rights workers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner were murdered in 1964, and spoke about “states’ rights,” a phrase that segregationists had adopted

In 1988, a pro-Bush group aired a commercial that attacked his Democratic opponent, Michael Dukakis, for allowing a convicted criminal named Wlliam Horton furlough from prison, during which he nearly killed someone

The ad didn’t mention Horton’s race and didn’t need to; it included his mugshot and called him “Willie,” which Horton (among others) interpreted as a dog whistle. “It was created to play on racial stereotypes: big, ugly, dumb, violent, Black—‘Willie,’” he said later

And, perhaps most relevant to the “Brad” brouhaha, Reagan often spoke about someone who became known as the “welfare queen.” As the journalist Josh Levin has written , this referred to a real individual, a woman in Chicago named Linda Taylor
Reagan never talked about her race, yet “welfare queen” became entrenched as a trope of lazy Black women grifting off the welfare system
This may explain why people such as Posobiec and Fishback are so agitated about the Arkansas ad: They understand how powerful a political weapon racial associations can be in shaping policy
But they don’t have Atwater’s finesse or plausible deniability
The right has gone from insisting that its rhetoric about entitlements was color-blind to demanding that it include racial signifiers
And though the number of Americans willing to tolerate or embrace gutter racism in politics appears to be growing, it remains a marginal group

The hardest-core activists, hyping one another up in group chats and on Discord servers, may have lost sight of that, failing to recognize how bizarre they look freaking out over a forgettable advertisement

If these identitarians looked around, they could see cautionary tales about the wholesale embrace of identity politics, such as the impression among many voters that the Democratic Party is more interested in niche groups than in ordinary people
They could learn from the first wave of the MAGA movement, which was willing to accommodate racism and bigotry for electoral gain but apparently believed that they could be contained and channeled
The commentator Erick Erickson, for example, has spent years tolerating Trumpism but now reacts with horror at neo-Nazis in the movement
Or they could consider the plight of Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who defended Trump’s every move from the White House lectern and now finds herself accused of treachery by his zealous followers

title: Trump Got What He Wanted From the Kennedy Center Honors
excerpt: The Kennedy Center Honors was once one of the biggest nights in Washington, which may not be saying much in a city that’s more blue blazer than red carpet
body: The Kennedy Center Honors was once one of the biggest nights in Washington, which may not be saying much in a city that’s more blue blazer than red carpet
Still, it was where D.C.’s buttoned-up power class got to mingle with Hollywood stars at an awards show that was broadcast to millions
Today the main building is closed and the organization has largely stopped presenting the arts
But once again this December, the Kennedy Center will put on a show
Officials announced today that the 49th Kennedy Center Honors will take place December 7 at Capital One Arena, the downtown stadium where Washington’s NBA and NHL teams play
At that point, the Kennedy Center will likely still be mired in a dispute in which its self-appointed chairman—Donald Trump—has said it might be demolished unless his name is added to the facade
Because of that drama, the Honors are poised to serve as something of a barometer of the institution
Under Trump, donors, artists, and audiences have fled from the center
And the most prominent tenants are discovering that they may function better away from it

Unable to perform at the Kennedy Center, the National Symphony Orchestra opened its new season to a grateful crowd in the Maryland suburbs last weekend and will spend the season seeking new audiences at six venues in the region
The Washington National Opera reported record fundraising hauls after ending its affiliation with the Kennedy Center earlier this year
But the Honors may prove harder to disentangle, because the show’s identity is inseparable from the Kennedy Center—and the Kennedy Center, in turn, has become inseparable from Trump
Trump’s issues with the ceremony go back to 2017, when several of the honorees spurned him
But last year, Trump made himself central to the event by selecting the awards recipients and becoming the first president to host the ceremony—at which he celebrated both the artists and himself
How involved he will be this time remains unclear; the White House did not respond to my questions about his plans
Also unclear is whether the Kennedy Center still has the cultural cachet to attract the level of talent it historically has drawn for the Honors

I posed that question to five people—former officials, staffers, and producers—who helped plan the Honors over the years, all of whom spoke with me on the condition of anonymity out of fear of professional repercussions

No matter what, they told me, it’s Trump’s show now, for better or worse. “It has gone from being the Kennedy Center to being about Donald Trump,” one person told me. “So in order to accept the Honor today, you have to be aligned with what he is doing.” Ordinarily, most of the details for the Kennedy Center Honors would have been firmed up by now—especially the recipients
Past organizers told me the ceremony required preparation year-round, starting even before the current year’s event raised its curtains
The selection process would begin in winter, and honorees were announced by the summer
But as October begins, the Kennedy Center has only now disclosed where and when the ceremony will occur
Last year, Trump said he handpicked the 2025 recipients: Sylvester Stallone, Gloria Gaynor, George Strait, Michael Crawford, and the rock band Kiss

Although the ceremony drew some Nashville heavyweights to honor Strait, the rest of the celebrity crowd was lighter on star power, and the biggest group of red-carpet walkers seemed to be Cabinet officials and their spouses

And this was before the biggest shock wave hit the institution: 12 days after the Honors, Trump’s name was installed on the building’s facade, which led to a new round of artists canceling appearances; later, Trump announced that he planned to close the institution for a renovation

A legal fight over the future of the center is still playing out in court. [ Read: What the Kennedy Center’s tax return reveals ] Speculating about who might be a realistic choice to accept a Kennedy Center Honor this year comes down to a relatively narrow set of criteria: someone accomplished, available, acceptable to Trump, and willing to receive the award from him

Maybe Jon Voight, whom the president honored with the National Medal of Arts in 2019 and recently named a “special ambassador” to Hollywood? Another such ambassador, and another plausible candidate, is Mel Gibson

Would the Honors turn to hip-hop stars such as Lil Wayne, whom Trump pardoned in 2021, or Nicki Minaj, who’s made a MAGA pivot in the past year? Either would be younger than the typical honoree, though their participation might boost ratings, which former producers tell me has always been a consideration in the selection process
Last year’s Honors, the first planned under Trump, saw ratings fall by about 25 percent from the previous year

Trump’s celebrity orbit offers plenty more options for a shortlist (last year he said he made his final picks from a list of about 50 names): The tenor Andrea Bocelli, who met with Trump in the Oval Office last year, wouldn’t feel out of place on an Honors roster

Kid Rock might, but he’s a longtime friend and supporter of the president. (Ditto Vanilla Ice ?) Or maybe the Village People, whose “YMCA” became such a standard of Trump rallies that the group performed at several events for the president’s second inauguration
The Honors have also lost much of the infrastructure behind the event
CBS’s deal to broadcast the show expired after the 2025 ceremony, and the network did not respond to my request for comment about this year
A Kennedy Center spokesperson told me that it would announce its broadcast partner later
Still, producing the Honors requires more than what viewers eventually see on television
Former officials described it to me as an all-campus effort, relying on staffers across multiple departments, including fundraising and special events

Many of those employees have left or been laid off ahead of the closure. “Uncertainty is the enemy of what’s going on here,” Senator Shelley Moore Capito, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, told me during an unrelated event this week hosted by Americans for the Arts

The West Virginia Republican wants to see the Honors return to the Kennedy Center eventually, but suggested that temporarily moving the ceremony elsewhere doesn’t need to be fatal. “Take one year and do it off campus and come back,” she said

At the same event, Kara Young, a two-time Tony Award–winning actress, told me the turmoil at the Kennedy Center has made celebrating art more necessary. “The truth is being silenced, and to me, art is truth,” she said

She added that if administration is “taking over places that are historically apolitical and historically for the arts, then people will find a way to seek what they need, which is the truth.” The Honors have proved adaptable before
During the pandemic, producers abandoned the typically packed Opera House to film segments across the Kennedy Center campus

title: Manipulator vs. Manipulator
excerpt: For a few minutes on Wednesday night, the New York Film Festival crowd watched Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced ex-CEO and founder of the medical start-up Theran
body: For a few minutes on Wednesday night, the New York Film Festival crowd watched Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced ex-CEO and founder of the medical start-up Theranos, and her partner, Billy Evans, as they seemingly went about their lives at a San Diego beach house
Evans was on the phone, insisting that nobody really understood Holmes; she sat next to him, her expression vacant, and patted her baby on the back
Moments later, she was talking with someone on her computer, her AirPods in and eyes unblinking
Then, suddenly, the camera cut to a third person—the comedian and director Nathan Fielder, who was observing from the side—prompting huge laughter from the crowd
Fielder was just standing there—not saying anything, not making a face, just existing in the room

But his appearance acknowledged something obvious: We were not watching a sober, straightforward accounting of Holmes’s domestic life in 2023, days before she was set to report to a federal prison on counts of defrauding investors in her company
To his fans, Fielder has cultivated a reputation as modern culture’s foremost stenographer of strange situations
Somehow, he had scored extensive access to a notorious fabulist whose moon-faced staring and affected baritone had made her a national punch line

And now, in You Can See Everything , the documentary that emerged out of the time he spent with Holmes, we were about to see just how weird this woman really was; the anticipation was unbearable, hence the laughter
You Can See Everything , made in collaboration with the director Lance Oppenheim, has gathered intense interest since its surprise reveal last month at the Telluride Film Festival

The standby line for tickets Wednesday stretched long and wide outside Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall, where the film would be playing; a publicist told me she’d heard that someone had been out there since 2:30 a.m
Inside, the director Noah Baumbach and the novelist Rachel Kushner took seats
The screening was the only one of the festival, and the last time the movie would be shown publicly ahead of its theatrical release, on October 16

Although some detailed reports about the movie had popped up after its screening at Telluride, Fielder and Oppenheim had apparently asked that crowd to not give away too much, and they did the same in a post-screening Q&A at NYFF
I’ll do my best. (You’ll have to find out for yourself why the movie earned an R rating for “some graphic nudity.”) In some ways, it’s easier to talk about what the movie isn’t
You Can See Everything lacks the architecture of Fielder’s best-known shows, where he establishes and solves an elaborate problem of his own making

Think of the second season of HBO’s The Rehearsal , during which Fielder wonders why airline pilots have a hard time communicating directly with one another—and, in his exploratory process, ends up becoming a certified pilot himself

In projects such as that show, and Comedy Central’s Nathan for You , he inhabits a quasi-fictional “Nathan Fielder” persona, who is droll and almost uncomfortably literal—possibly neurodivergent, as explored in an episode on The Rehearsal
What he’s doing in You Can See Everything is closer to journalism

The filming constituted Holmes’s first exposure to the media in seven years , and Fielder—amazingly, preposterously—was one of the few people on the planet (she also did an interview with The New York Times ) in a position to chip away at some of Holmes’s self-evident fictions, a privilege he took seriously
He does not appear to be inhabiting a persona; initially, he told the New York audience, he wasn’t even supposed to appear on-screen

The documentary is filled with scenes in which Fielder deliberates with his collaborators about a potential line of inquiry, or aggressively presses Holmes or Evans in the hope of catching them fibbing about one of their many boisterous claims. [ Read: Elizabeth Holmes isn’t fooling anyone ] Frustratingly for him, Holmes is a world-class prevaricator
She is a convicted felon, a newish mother, in a happy relationship—all positions that can transform how a person moves through the world, yet the facade never drops
Up close, the public stereotypes around her persona are largely confirmed
At one point she insists, with total sincerity, that not only is she always being honest, but she has never told a lie in her life
Hearing this, Fielder’s stoicism cracks; he’s as openly baffled as viewers may be

Faced with such willful obstinacy, he attempts a more indirect fact-finding mission, working his way backwards from some of Holmes’s contentions to understand how she distinguishes between a truth and a lie
For example, the documentary spends some time unpacking Theranos’s well-publicized claim that it had created a machine that could perform more than 1,000 diagnostic medical tests
To be clear: This was not true, at all, and was extensively debunked
But Fielder keeps nudging Holmes to clarify how she came to believe she was telling the truth
In her eyes, Holmes slowly explains, the machine itself was theoretically capable of performing these tests, only the company hadn’t developed the actual tests

Again, to be clear: This is sophistry, like claiming you’ve invented a car that’s theoretically capable of driving at 10,000 miles an hour … only the necessary engine doesn’t exist, and you know it doesn’t exist
Fielder continues pushing, leading Holmes to quietly withdraw; she seems genuinely shell-shocked by the growing impossibility of justifying her position out loud
Inquisitive moments like these are seemingly the closest she comes to grasping that her reasoning doesn’t stack up

Meanwhile, Evans simmers with badly concealed irritation over Fielder’s skepticism. “I know what you’re feeling,” he interjects at the end of this long explanation, only for Fielder to respond, quickly and forcefully, “No, you don’t.” This has been one of the recurring themes of Fielder’s work: the difficulty of really seeing inside someone else’s head, of authentically connecting with another person

His shows are filled with people who appear to have never thought through their worldview using their words—who, when they try, do such a bad job of it that Fielder can typically respond only with his trademark deadpan “Oh, okay” (a phrase that pops up in this film)

In letting his subjects speak for themselves, he elicits the easy laugh at the obviously ridiculous, like a man on The Rehearsal who’s obsessed with numerology and won’t stop talking about how he crashed his Scion tC
But his works remind viewers that not all things under the sun abide by rationale and common sense
Some of them squirrel away in a cave of their own making for years and years, never exposing their beliefs to sunlight
Others are convinced they’ve got something special to share with the world—and, when they try to do so, slowly erect the circumstances of their own downfall

title: An Argument Against AI Doom
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The flood of reports about AI agents escaping and hacking websites can feel scary
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The flood of reports about AI agents escaping and hacking websites can feel scary
But is this actually just a matter of needing better security to match the evolving technology? Zack Korman, the CEO of Embroidery, thinks so
He works in cybersecurity and argues that “rogue” AI agents are less frightening and complicated than they may seem
Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks with Korman about how companies and institutions should up their cyberdefenses and why the so-called AI doomers are frustrating him
The following is a transcript of the episode: Zack Korman: I think that realistically, what will happen is models will get better
And if the labs do not up their cybersecurity game, and if the companies running AI agents do not up their cybersecurity game, they will cause real harm
And then we will literally get them in trouble
Like, we will put someone in prison because you killed people
And the doomers would say, No —but then it’s too late, because they’re afraid that the people we killed would be like 8 billion, whereas I’m not
I’m like, No —because that’s not the real world; it doesn’t work like this
Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna calibrate our anxiety about the AI-hacking epidemic
Specifically, we’re going to answer the question: Is the rogue-AI-agent problem really just a normal cybersecurity issue, or is it something else altogether? It’s a scary moment
As we’re recording this on September 29, the news is moving quite fast
But allow me to summarize some of the broader points
Since August, there’s been a pretty steady drumbeat of revelations, starting with OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face during a training exercise
Agents hacked into a German website to use it as a rudimentary message board
An agent for OpenAI gained unauthorized access to a data portal that was run by Australia’s universal health-care insurance provider
And last week, OpenAI revealed that its models attempted to hack or otherwise access numerous U.S.-government websites
That same day, OpenAI announced that 53 incidences happened where photos were uploaded by users to the company via its products, which were then uploaded without permission onto other platforms

Last weekend, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic were looking at tens of thousands of potential incidences where agents were behaving in unexpected ways—either coordinating or trying to get around, or succeeding in getting around company guardrails and causing problems on the open internet
This week, OpenAI announced it was pausing training of its most capable models and delaying the release of its newest model, citing security concerns
But let’s be clear; these are very real examples of technologists losing control or being unable to monitor their tools
And there’s lots of talk about what kind of liability these companies ought to face
Whether these types of hacks are subject to penalties under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
Online, there’s been a constant debate over what is going on, why nobody has been held accountable, what accountability means, and what needs to happen next

But all that chatter and all this news has merged with a different narrative online—the one that is best represented by the AI safety-and-doomer camp, and the fears that an out-of-control, self-improving AI system could one day “kill us all.” But these are, in a way, two different stories
One is about a hypothetical, improved set of models
It’s a frightening scenario, but it is speculative
The second story—the one of the AI-agent hacks—is not speculative
It is something that is happening right now, and it is both urgent and it is tangible
And my guest today, Zack Korman, argues that this is a problem that is not sci-fi in nature
That we are not dealing with machine gods with agency, but with a sprawling cybersecurity problem, and the companies are acting negligently
Korman runs Embroidery, an AI-agent monitoring-and-detection platform, and so I wanted to have him on to talk about what’s really going on here with these high-profile hacks
Can we constrain these agents? If so, how? What are the real risks involved with agentic AI, and how do we keep them from coming to pass? Korman joins me now to talk about it all
Warzel: All right, Zack, welcome to Galaxy Brain

Warzel: So we are talking here on September 29, after a weekend where there’s been a lot of news, mostly about OpenAI agents accessing outside systems, some inside the U.S. government without authorization
I imagine if you are somebody who doesn’t have a background in AI or cybersecurity, you are looking at this like we have entered some kind of nightmare scenario
You, however, work in cybersecurity and AI, so just let’s set the table here
What is your broad reaction to all of this news that has transpired over the past week? Korman: Yeah; I mean it’s not as scary as it sounds
One of the core challenges of working in cybersecurity and suddenly having cybersecurity be a dramatic topic is that for people in cybersecurity, like—everything has been bad forever

title: A Mysterious Literary Pattern
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books

Some publishing trends so clearly reflect cultural changes that they are easy to explain: Few readers in 2026 are surprised by, say, a sudden crop of books about artificial intelligence, or a best-selling series of novels catering to young gamers
Other literary patterns are more mysterious
Klein wrote about Robert Kolker’s The Vanishing Family , which adds to a growing bookshelf of new works focusing on dementia
Klein’s essay led me to wonder why several notable recent releases, both nonfiction and novels, have taken on this condition—and how each explores the subject differently

First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section: What Vienna lost when it lost its Jews The best seller that’s nearly impossible to finish reading A dissatisfying apocalypse Literature is becoming more like a video game

One reason people are spending so much time alone “Drawing the Birds Back Into the Sky,” a poem by Trish Reeves The Vanishing Family follows a clan dealing with an inherited form of dementia that drastically changes the sufferer’s personality

Klein is most interested in Kolker’s emphasis on the “slipperiness of identity” and the “malleability of the self”; are you still the same person without your usual behaviors or your formative memories? As some family members succumb to the condition, the author also focuses on their healthy caregivers, for whom “the sense of loss is ongoing—like witnessing a living death.” The mysteries of dementia—both medical and personal, for both patient and loved ones—provide rich terrain for writers, as Marion Renault pointed out last year in a different Atlantic essay about the book Valley of Forgetting , by Jennie Erin Smith

We know very little about the condition, but at the same time, it comes with a “grim certainty”—it is largely untreatable, and always terminal. “This tension makes the illness ripe for figurative language,” Renault wrote
Both Kolker and Smith conveyed this tension in fine writing and painstaking detail, but figurative language is where fiction excels
This year, two novels managed to approach the illness in new ways—one from the perspective of a caregiver and another from a patient’s point of view
Kenan Orhan’s The Renovation is a somewhat surrealist fable about many things—exile, autocracy, the nuclear family, the carceral state
But the greatest stressor in the life of its protagonist, Dilara, is her father’s rapidly progressing Alzheimer’s

Orhan portrays the hard realities of caring for someone you no longer recognize, but also explores the metaphorical possibilities: Dilara and her father were forced to flee Turkey as political refugees, and they both yearn for a past that has become inaccessible, whether or not they remember it

In her stark new novel, Switzy , Emma Cline gives us the perspective of the sufferer. “Alzheimer’s novels are rare,” Hillary Kelly wrote in an Atlantic essay about the book, “and those told from the patient’s point of view are rarer.” Cline portrays her subject, David, “in a wandering, dreamlike style,” Kelly writes

His mental absence “becomes a startling and eerie phenomenon—like the moment you realize you’ve been driving for miles but don’t recall anything about the journey.” David is flying to Zurich in a private jet so that he can die by assisted suicide before Alzheimer’s robs him of his agency
As he rifles through half memories and smiles through painful interactions, Cline expertly dramatizes the tension Renault defined between the unknowableness of dementia and its unavoidable end
David is becoming a different person, but for now he is still himself, and he holds on desperately to the single choice he has left
Alzheimer’s novels are not so rare anymore, but like any great novelist, Cline has found a wholly original way to distinguish her work
Corbis Historical / Getty The Mysteries of Human Personality By Julia M
Klein Robert Kolker’s latest book, The Vanishing Family , tracks the effects of inherited dementia and the many transformations that follow

What to Read Dad Brain , by Darby Saxbe Saxbe, a clinical psychologist and professor, has been “endlessly curious about how fathers tick” since she was in elementary school, when her parents’ divorce—and equal custody split—turned her detached dad into a terrific parent
Now she’s one of the only scientists in the world who researches the neurological effects of fatherhood
Some of her collaborators have already shown that pregnancy alters a mom’s hormones and brain structure in ways that are good for bonding and child-rearing
Saxbe’s work demonstrates that tending to infants triggers similar neurological changes in other parents—and that the more time they spend on child care, the larger these shifts tend to be

She explains her discoveries in chatty, accessible language, mixing in social science that often contains useful tips; for example, greater paternal involvement at bedtime is correlated with better baby and toddler sleep. (Maybe that’s why my 2-year-old always demands, “Go with Daddy tonight?”) But the most thrilling part of Dad Brain is its overall conclusion: that “great parents are made, not born.” — Lily Meyer From our list: The summer reading guide Out Next Week 📚 The Savage Mind , by David Treuer 📚 Partita , by Barbara Kingsolver 📚 Every Story Is a Love Story , by Imbolo Mbue Your Weekend Read Illustration by Colin Hunter / The Atlantic

title: Is There Anything Kash Patel Won’t Do for Trump Before the Midterms?
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter

E arlier this year , FBI Director Kash Patel vowed before God, Fox Nation, and Donald Trump that he would punish the “deep state” for its manifold transgressions, especially the (actually nonexistent) conspiracy to steal the 2020 election. “I’ve been with the president nearly since day one on this,” he said in an interview with Maria Bartiromo. “I can announce on your show that we’ve got all the information we need

We’re working with our prosecutors at the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche, and we are going to be making arrests, and it’s coming, and I promise you, it’s coming soon.” That was five months ago
Patel has not yet delivered on his promise

But in interviews with more than 40 current and former administration officials, FBI employees, and members of Congress and their staffers, as well as others close to the White House, I’ve learned that it is not for lack of trying
The people I spoke with described Patel as desperate to help the Justice Department indict putative malefactors and stimulate headlines to please the president
Nearly all of the people I spoke with would speak only on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation if their name appeared in the story

Patel has filed a $250 million defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic and me in response to my reporting earlier this year that he has alarmed colleagues with episodes of excessive drinking and unexplained absences
In recent months, Patel has been briefed on the FBI’s “election integrity” investigations in Arizona, Florida, New Jersey, Ohio, and beyond

Officials told me their understanding is that many of the election-related investigation requests came directly from the White House, many times with the instruction that “this is a big deal for the president” or “this is a push from 47.” But all of that attention hasn’t yielded results
In meetings, Patel has expressed frustration that there have been no new findings, and instructed staff to “look harder” or “look again,” according to three people familiar with the conversations
The FBI’s preoccupation with the 2020 election represents a dramatic break with its past

Though the bureau—one of the world’s most famous and most powerful law-enforcement agencies—has experienced more than its share of controversies and episodes of overreach, it has also been dedicated to criminal investigation based in evidence, science, and reality
The commitment of personnel, resources, and time to investigate a conspiracy theory that was manufactured by Trump to explain his electoral defeat marks a decisive pivot away from its historical role
Patel’s aggressive pursuit of the conspiracy investigation has helped him keep his job
Reports that Trump is keen to push him out have diminished

Patel’s predecessors had always sought to demonstrate their independence by creating operational and optical distance from the White House—especially when it came to the sanctity and neutrality of elections

Patel has taken a radically different course, attempting to translate Trump’s eternal election-related grievances into a core law-enforcement mission of the federal government. “Patel is the only guy who never says no,” a Republican operative close to the White House told me. “And the president likes that.” [ Read: Trump’s purge may be just beginning ] In response to a three-page memo I wrote outlining 17 detailed questions for him regarding the FBI’s pivot to election-conspiracy investigations, Patel responded in a most curious fashion
Instead of addressing my questions, he wrote: “I’m still looking for my gold-plated jet ski in the English Channel; you all know where it is
Free ride if you help me find it.” I did not understand this response
I have never written about, or asked Patel or the FBI about, anything having to do with Jet Skis or the English Channel
A bit of Googling, however, uncovered the probable root of his reply
On July 10, MS NOW published a story concerning Patel’s political difficulties, some of which, the story said, related to his lifestyle
Included in the story was a graphic of, among other things, a white Jet Ski, a set of golf clubs, and a private jet

Patel responded to the MS NOW story on X, writing, “Nah, my jet ski is gold plated… dumbass.” Put simply, Patel responded to The Atlantic ’s questions about the FBI’s election investigations by referring to a graphic that appeared on an unrelated news story on another media company’s website
Other FBI officials, however, did respond to my questions

The FBI’s press office sent me statements from five other named officials—Chris Raia, Andrew Bailey, Chad Yarborough, Joe Perez, and Matt Fodor—who defended Patel, claimed my reporting was “false,” and insisted that the FBI was “united.” Many of the statements used almost-identical language and did not deny that the FBI was focused on the alleged election conspiracy
The FBI published my questions and its answers on X last night, before this story was published

A spokesperson for the FBI said in a statement that “election security is and will continue to be one of this FBI’s highest national security priorities, and we will make no apologies for any work to ensure every American citizen’s sacred right to vote is protected from criminal interference.” The spokesperson said there has been a “500% increase in election integrity related investigations and arrests just this year alone” and denied that there had been any internal concerns raised about the bureau’s approach to election-related investigations
But others I spoke with told me that Patel’s stance is redefining how the bureau prepares for an election
One striking example came last month when FBI and DOJ staff attended an “election integrity” training session
In the past, these trainings have focused on how to respond to the most common threats to poll workers or voting locations

Some attendees were alarmed that a focus of this year’s training was about voting by undocumented immigrants, a statistically rare phenomenon that has nevertheless preoccupied Trump and others on the right
There was little mention of the prohibition on armed federal law enforcement being stationed at the polls

Agents across the country have been seeking counsel in recent weeks about how to respond to FBI directives related to the election, according to six current and former FBI and DOJ supervisors and outside defense attorneys who told me they have received calls. “Agents are nervous, talking among themselves,” said a former DOJ official who has received multiple requests for advice unlike anything this person has seen before

Another former senior FBI official told me he had received calls from dozens of his former colleagues looking for counsel and describing “a real effort to bend people to the narrative” of the president’s election-conspiracy theories
One agent told me he contemplates Election Day and thinks: “I’m either gonna be sick that day or they are going to have to fire me.” There is no question that people in the FBI are rattled
What is uncertain is the degree to which they should be
On Monday, Andrew Bailey, one of the FBI’s co–deputy directors, unexpectedly announced that he was leaving the bureau, citing a desire to spend more time with his family
Bailey had overseen election-related investigations, and had supported Trump’s false fraud claims

title: Redefining enterprise intelligence with autonomous AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition
body: Enterprise AI is no longer a future ambition
Model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can absorb, while the cost of performance continues to fall
Globally, AI investment is set to reach $2.5 trillion in 2026, up 44% from the previous year
For many enterprises, this investment has produced fragmentation

Intelligence can accumulate in silos so that sales agents are unaware of open support tickets, for instance, or marketing systems are personalizing content without visibility into what finance already knows about a customer
Each function may perform well in isolation, but the enterprise as a whole learns little and has less information to act upon

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT The shift from AI as a tool to AI as an operating model—what we call the “agentic shift” in this report—demands something more fundamental than better models or faster infrastructure
It requires connecting people, processes, and data in real time, along with the governance and control to act on that intelligence reliably
This means rethinking both architecture and operating models simultaneously
First, rebuilding data infrastructure for accessibility rather than volume
Second, replacing fixed tech stacks with composable architectures that can evolve as models and tools change
And, lastly, resolving questions of AI sovereignty, including where intelligence runs, who controls it, and how it operates across organizational and jurisdictional boundaries
Key findings include the following: Enterprise AI’s scaling problem is structural
Process-first companies are pulling ahead
Global AI spending is rising sharply and model capabilities are advancing faster than most organizations can integrate them
Yet the majority of enterprises are still not growing revenue through AI or fundamentally rethinking how they operate
The companies generating sustained returns share a common discipline
They treat process redesign as the work that precedes model selection, building for how the technology will evolve rather than retrofitting roles and workflows after deployment
For them, the agentic shift begins with the operating model
Data readiness, not data abundance, is what makes AI compoundable
Most enterprises discover too late that having data and having AI-ready data are very different things
A sovereign, composable foundation—one that queries and prepares data where it resides, without migration or centralization—can convert raw data estates into intelligence that AI agents can act upon

As data residency laws, multicloud environments, and structural complexity make centralization increasingly impractical, sovereign control over where models run and data lives is what keeps that adaptability intact

It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: A new contest pits competitors against each other in a race to biological youth
excerpt: Biological age as a competition: A new six-month contest called pits around 500 participants against each other to reverse their biological age, using tools lik
body: Biological age as a competition: A new six-month contest called pits around 500 participants against each other to reverse their biological age, using tools like epigenetic blood tests, brain scans, face-aging apps, and grip strength measurements

The science is promising but imperfect: Over 100 biological "aging clocks" exist, but experts caution they aren't yet reliable enough for individual use—nobody fully understands what each one actually measures

Data collection is a goal: Founder Christin Glorioso hopes the contest generates the world's most comprehensive aging-clock dataset, while also giving longevity companies a cheaper alternative to running formal clinical trials

The leaderboard is shaping up: One competitor's biological age clocks in nearly 29 years below their chronological age—while another 47-year-old received a biological age of 100 based on how slowly she rises from a chair " data-chronoton-post-id="1145610" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This week, I officially signed up for an unusual competition
One that rewards competitors for getting younger
I recently turned 40, and I don’t need reminding that both time and my chronological age only tick forward
But this game is focused on competitors’ biological ages—figures that are meant to provide a better way to measure the age-related health of our organs and bodies
Over a six-month period, around 500 of us will try to reverse our biological age as measured in a bunch of different ways

There’s even a leaderboard! The winners will include the person who shows the greatest difference between their chronological and biological age, as well as the person who manages to reverse their biological age the most
The competition is the brainchild of the neuroscientist and physician Christin Glorioso, who is also founder and CEO of NeuroAge Therapeutics
The company offers tools to track brain health and aging and is running a trial to find out if biological brain age can predict the onset of Alzheimer’s disease
Glorioso says she has several goals for the Younger contest

The first, she tells me, is to “explain to the world what aging clocks are.” Regular Checkup readers will be familiar with these tools, but for the uninitiated, they are basically designed to measure biological age
Many measure chemical signatures that form a layer on top of our DNA and seem to change with age
But others might involve looking at proteins or lipids in blood
Some are designed to measure functional health, while others predict when a person will die
There are more than a hundred clocks out there, and they probably each capture a specific aspect of the biological process of aging
These clocks are proving very useful for scientists , who use them to study aging and development in humans and many other species
But using them to estimate the biological age of an individual person is more controversial
They’re just not good enough for that yet
Part of the problem is that we don’t really understand what each clock is capturing
Glorioso hopes that data collected through the Younger contest might help answer that question
She’s hoping to generate “the world’s most comprehensive clock dataset.” Some longevity clinics try to get around the limits of biological age testing by using multiple clocks

As a standard competitor, I’ll be sending a blood spot sample to TruDiagnostic, a company that measures epigenetic chemical groups on DNA and offers to reveal an overall biological age as well as a person’s pace of aging and the biological ages of each of 11 organ systems, including the heart and brain
I’ll get a brain age score from NeuroAge once I complete the cognitive tasks on offer
I’ll also submit some physical measures like grip strength
And I’ll upload a series of selfies to an app developed by a team at Harvard that promises to tell me my face age
That’s exactly what it sounds like—an estimate of how old my face looks
I’m intrigued to see my scores, even though I know I shouldn’t put too much stock in them
The first time I took a test, four years ago, the company I used gave me a biological age that matched my chronological age, which was a little disappointing and, if I’m honest, a bit underwhelming
A year later, the same company told me I had a young heart but a relatively old brain, liver, and hormonal system
My lifestyle hasn’t changed much since then

Will the years have made much difference? (Ultra competitors—who pay $4,499 rather than the $999 cost of regular entry—are also offered a range of other blood tests and clocks, as well as MRI and DEXA scans
I’ve got complimentary press access to the standard package.) Glorioso is also hoping to gather information about the effects of some purported longevity approaches

During the competition, some participants will be offered red-light masks, access to a sauna, or other low-risk offerings that partner companies who are sponsoring the event to varying degrees might want to collect data on. “A lot of these companies just can’t afford to run [clinical] trials,” says Glorioso
She also sees the event as a public health initiative

A couple of years ago, David Sinclair, who studies aging at Harvard Medical School, and his colleagues estimated that if we could slow down aging in the general population and increase life expectancy by one year, it would save the US economy $38 trillion
The event officially kicks off in January, but around 120 people have already signed up, says Glorioso
Each person’s six-month run starts as soon as they take their baseline measurements, whenever that may be

A handful of people have already started. “I think the majority of people are going to want to sign up after the holidays,” says Glorioso. “They’re not going to want to be trying to win an aging contest over Christmas and Hanukkah.” Glorioso took her own baseline measurements back in August

title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
excerpt: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human o
body: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent
Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch

AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time. “I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine,” Lee said afterwards . “But when I saw this move, I changed my mind

Surely, AlphaGo is creative.” When Deep Blue defeated then reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard-coded by humans
A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves
Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years
To win, AlphaGo had to sense who was ahead at a glance and even invent moves no human had thought to play
That is why many accounts of AlphaGo’s match against Lee portray move 37 as a flash of pure machine intuition
It was actually AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks
If we want future AI systems to produce trustworthy results and really novel insights in fields like science and medicine, we need to equip them with genuine reasoning capabilities of this kind
The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play
This “intuitive” part regarded move 37 as nothing special—a play that had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player
What made AlphaGo choose it was the program’s search machinery, which looked beyond immediate plausibility and weighed the future consequences of proposed moves

It explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.  A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 is fast, gut-level, effortless; system 2, slow, step-by-step, and deliberative
AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split

Its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow
As in human cognition, neither half works alone
Intuition alone would never have opted for move 37, and brute-force search would have struggled to sieve through all the many possible moves
This is strikingly different from the way today’s AI models work
A large language model picks the next token, over and over
That amounts to system 1 in action—fast, associative, and surprisingly good pattern completion across almost every subject people write about
Not long after ChatGPT debuted, the field realized that language fluency alone falls short of true usefulness

The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate: Instead of answering immediately, they can now generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning—a process known as chain of thought
The gains have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding

But unlike AlphaGo’s search, this does not introduce a genuinely separate reasoning mechanism: The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next-token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer
Three shortcomings prevent what chatbots do from qualifying as reasoning (in a way that a scientist might recognize)
First, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state

There is no open ledger that lays out the hypotheses a model is considering, the confidence it has in various explanations, the evidence it’s weighing, and the unresolved questions it’s holding onto—all things that should be systematically revised as new information arrives
Second, they lack a clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge
Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs

Third, while the chains of thought chatbots produce look like deliberation, research has demonstrated that the bots often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another

This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications we all care about, such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research, it matters not only what a system concludes but also how it arrives at its conclusion

When mistakes happen—for example, in medical diagnosis and treatment—we need to be able to pinpoint what went wrong: Was the system’s reasoning at fault, did it draw on invalid evidence, or did it make incorrect assumptions?  This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind
I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning—one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture
AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree
This data structure contains all the variations, the possible futures, that AlphaGo has considered, each move and position being annotated with judgments made by its neural networks

As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo updates the game tree and eventually synthesizes the information in it to decide which move to make.  Similarly, for general reasoning a system should maintain an epistemic state that represents what the system holds as settled, what it doubts, what it has ruled out, which questions stay open

Reasoning can then be understood as a sequence of moves that change the epistemic state to advance knowledge and reduce uncertainty: deducing consequences, breaking problems into parts, and—crucially—deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next
Of course, open-world reasoning is harder than playing a board game such as Go or chess

In the real world the current state of affairs is only partially known, the set of available actions is large and variable, and the consequences of actions are stochastic or unknown.  But recent advances in LLMs and other neural models now give us the capability to take on such general reasoning problems

title: Cornell 7 case puts a spotlight on fraternity misconduct – and the limits of universities’ power to stop it
url:
<title>Cornell 7 case puts a spotlight on fraternity misconduct – and the limits of universities’ power to stop it</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763447/original/file-20261001-60-53vxfr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A case alleging that a Cornell sophomore was sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members is drawing national attention.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/students-walk-and-ride-across-the-campus-of-cornell-news-photo/2297900593?phrase=cornell%20university%20campus&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Universities have been trying for years to cut back on the abuses among fraternities, with limited resources and limited success.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf">new lawsuit</a>, filed by a former Cornell University student in September 2026, is now rattling higher education and <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-lede/how-the-cornell-seven-rape-case-became-a-national-scandal">drawing national attention</a>.</p>

<p>The person, identified as Jane Doe, has alleged that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and gang-raped her at an on-campus fraternity house when she was a sophomore in 2024.</p>

<p>Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to pursue criminal charges against the fraternity members in 2024. Following the filing of the case and emergence of new information, however, Van Houten <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/nyregion/van-houten-cornell-district-attorney.html">said on Sept. 26 that he is planning</a> “to discuss new evidence that exists” with the former Cornell student about her sexual assault claims. </p>

<p>The high-profile Cornell case is <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/wisconsin-fraternity-hazing-basement-rcna599852">just one of the latest</a> <a href="https://apnews.com/article/arizona-fraternity-pledge-hazing-death-b53c547d383082d33aebdb4950e0c550">fraternity scandals</a>. In August 2026, Pennsylvania announced <a href="https://www.psu.edu/news/campus-life/story/penn-state-responds-serious-criminal-charges-against-current-and-former-students">charges against current and former Penn State fraternity members</a> for their involvement in a criminal narcotics operation. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.drsasso.com/">education scholar</a> who researches the experiences of undergraduate college students and fraternities, I believe that universities and colleges have not devoted enough resources toward <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/ijamh.2012.012">curtailing the hazing</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10778012211037381">sexual assault</a> and other kinds of dangerous behavior that sometimes happens at fraternities or other student organizations. </p>

<p>But there is only so much they can do – in part because beneath it all is a hypermasculine culture of proving one’s worth.</p>

<h2>A need for more enforcement</h2>

<p>In 1984, the National Minimum Drinking Age Act pressured states to set 21 as the minimum age to <a href="https://alcoholpolicy.niaaa.nih.gov/the-1984-national-minimum-drinking-age-act">purchase and consume alcohol</a>. All states made <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/23/158">21 the minimum age</a> by 1988. </p>

<p>The change meant that most college students could no longer legally purchase alcohol, leading some of them to drink in more private settings, like fraternity houses.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-04-28-mn-1607-story.html?">Some universities</a> felt concerned about the alcohol-related injuries and deaths occurring at fraternity houses. Schools also faced the possibility of <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/1990/524-pa-356-1.html?">lawsuits over underage</a> drinking.  </p>

<p>Harmful binge drinking remained a major problem on college campuses throughout the <a href="https://doi.org/10.15288/jsa.2002.63.136">1990s and early 2000s</a>. A lot of the documented hazing incidents <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9782661/">at fraternities during this time also involved alcohol</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20249">Sexual assault on college campuses</a>, including at fraternities, was another major issue during this time.</p>

<p>A lot of universities started to respond to students’ excessive alcohol use, in part <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10410236.2023.2212447">through social norming</a>. This term means correcting people’s mistaken beliefs about what their peers normally do, like regularly drinking excessively. </p>

<p>They also tried other <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07448481.2021.1927048">harm-reduction strategies</a>, like sharing direct information with students about the negative effects of consuming alcohol, as well as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/hsc.13990">peer-led interventions</a> to try to reduce unsafe drinking or encourage alcohol moderation. </p>

<p>But they didn’t necessarily respond to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07448481.2021.2024210">related problems</a> surrounding hazing, such as substance misuse or addiction.</p>

<p>Some of the students’ parents, including those who had children who <a href="https://abcnews.com/GMA/News/parents-hazing-victims-react-house-passage-stop-campus/story?id=114075194">died as a result of hazing</a>, were concerned. They <a href="https://www.antihazingcoalition.org/about/">developed a large, nationwide parent lobby</a> to <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/parents-lobby-for-anti-hazing-bill/565684/">advocate for changes</a> in hazing laws across states. These groups, not the universities, have <a href="https://www.seattletimes.com/education-lab/biden-signs-anti-hazing-bill-backed-by-wa-parents/">been the most influential</a> in advocating for changes in hazing laws. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Some prevention efforts</h2>

<p>It’s not that some universities haven’t tried to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20528">reduce hazing on their campuses</a>. These efforts include practices such as hosting educational sessions, workshops, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ss.20524">speakers and even placing moratoriums</a> on social fraternity events that include alcohol. </p>

<p>Recent approaches have included teaching <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/csj.2016.0018">students how to recognize when their peers are emotionally distressed</a> and need help. </p>

<p>Some universities have started <a href="https://piazzacenter.psu.edu/who-we-are-piazza-history/">research centers on hazing</a> or hired full-time staff <a href="https://www.k-state.edu/student-support/conduct/hazing/">members whose jobs</a> <a href="https://www.health.columbia.edu/content/sexual-violence-response-staff-directory">involve prevention</a> and <a href="https://www.wm.edu/offices/wellness/ohp/violence-prevention/">response work</a> following a harmful incident such as hazing or sexual violence.</p>

<h2>Limited responses</h2>

<p>Universities can kick fraternities off campus and kick out athletes who are charged with <a href="https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/Page?handle=hein.journals/mqslr26&amp;div=32&amp;g_sent=1&amp;casa_token=&amp;collection=journals">hazing or sexual assault</a>. </p>

<p>But fraternities can also exist as private organizations, independent of a university. A university can withdraw recognition from a fraternity chapter and prohibit it from hosting events on campus, but that does not necessarily prevent the organization from <a href="https://myersedpress.presswarehouse.com/browse/book/9781975502645/Foundations-Research-and-Assessment-of-Fraternities-and-Sororities">hosting gatherings off campus</a>. </p>

<p>Another issue is that universities and colleges like Cornell have a civil process for dealing with hazing and other crimes, including sexual assault, but <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1079063217750864">not a criminal one</a>. Schools cannot <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0886260520925789">launch a criminal investigation</a>, but they can levy educational sanctions, including banning students from campus or taking away students’ scholarships. </p>

<p>Expelling students for illegal misconduct such as sexual assault and hazing is a really common approach, but that is about as far as these schools can go in terms of discipline.  </p>

<p>Schools may also cooperate with criminal investigations. Campus police, for example, can share their evidence and records with outside law enforcement. Or university staff may testify against students in court. But universities themselves cannot bring criminal charges. </p>

<p>After Jane Doe <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/doe-cornell-new-york-supreme.pdf">reported the incident</a> to university police, Cornell says it took action. </p>

<p>In a September 2026 statement, Cornell said its range of sanctions included “<a href="https://statements.cornell.edu/2026/20260928-da-investigation.cfm">expulsions and suspensions</a>.” A few students were asked to write essays, but Cornell says this wasn’t “as a sole consequence of their involvement.” </p>

<p>The Chi Phi chapter involved in the incident was also closed in 2024, according to Cornell. </p>

<p>Following the lawsuit and recent national attention it received, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/cornell-rape-allegations-investigation-7073e8da8b027fe9ee4530ea8a549f64">Cornell agreed to bring in</a> outside lawyers to determine whether it properly conducted the 2024 rape investigation. </p>

<h2>The role of masculinity</h2>

<p>Proving your masculinity <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/19496591.2019.1669455">can become a central part of proving your worth</a> and <a href="https://journal.libraries.wm.edu/jsflrp/article/view/730">fit at a fraternity</a>.</p>

<p>This <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10810730.2023.2222077">hypermasculine culture</a> – combined with a culture of secrecy – could be a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1097184X221133122">powder keg for sexual violence</a>. It’s a dynamic also seen <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.focus.20170024">in the military</a> and on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/08862605231178356">sports teams</a>.</p>

<p>Hypermasculinity is not simply tied up in an individual’s behavior, but can become embedded within organizational cultures that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/19496591.2019.1669455">reward toughness, dominance, risk-taking and silence</a>. </p>

<p>In fraternities, these expectations may shape how members understand belonging and status. These issues may <a href="https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/men0000375">also discourage students</a> from <a href="https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/men0000180">expressing vulnerability</a> and seeking help. </p>

<p>Understanding these gendered and cultural dynamics is, I believe, essential to developing prevention efforts that address not only individual conduct, but also the organizational norms that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1353/csd.2016.0079">allow harmful behaviors to persist</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293305/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>US regulators want to make corporate earnings reports less frequent, but investors have doubts</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763465/original/file-20261001-50-ym9m1p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8502%2C5668&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A new financial reporting proposal, pitched by Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins, has generated enormous opposition, from ordinary savers to industry groups.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=securities%20and%20exchange%20commission&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The U.S. government has pitched an obscure accounting rule change that has ignited <a href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/regulation/sec-quarterly-earnings-reports-complaints-2979d5a0">a firestorm</a> of opposition. If enacted, its effects might be felt from the capital markets to your retirement savings account.</p>

<p>At issue is <a href="https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026-42-sec-proposes-amendments-permit-optional-semiannual-reporting-public-companies">a proposal</a> by the <a href="https://www.sec.gov/">Securities and Exchange Commission</a> that would scrap a long-standing requirement for registered companies to disclose their earnings every three months. Instead, they would have the option to do so only every six months.</p>

<p>The agency says its <a href="https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/atkins-statement-proposing-release-semiannual-reporting-050526">proposal has two goals</a>: One is to reduce a company’s compliance costs needed to prepare financial statements; the other is to promote longer-term planning rather than a short-term fixation on earnings. A final decision is expected by late 2026.</p>

<p>These ideas may sound in the weeds to the average American, but the proposal has prompted opposition that is literally record-breaking ever since it was released for comments in May 2026. To date, <a href="https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/news/sec-faces-delays-on-semiannual-reporting-proposal-amid-record-number-of-comment-letters/">over 280,000 letters</a> have come in, with the vast majority against. By comparison, <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6717658">one study</a> that covered 417 different proposals over 30 years tallied more than 65,000 letters total.</p>

<p>I’m an accounting professor who has constructed <a href="https://tzachizach.github.io/sec-semi-annual-proposal-tracker/index.html">a tracker</a> that lets people scour the SEC docket and decipher the general sentiment of these comments. I found that the main driver of this hostility is concern that less frequent reporting would make it harder for investors to monitor companies’ performance and decision-making, because key information is withheld for longer periods. </p>

<p>This reduction in transparency carries another risk as well: It would likely make it more expensive for companies to raise capital. Once external monitoring is reduced, investors may demand a <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/248475">higher rate of return</a> because they have less information about the company’s health. That means the company would need to pay more for that uncertainty, whether through selling shares, borrowing from lenders or issuing bonds. </p>

<p>In short, there’s a trade-off between the cost of capital and transparency.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A photo image shows financial information on a computer screen." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763491/original/file-20261001-50-lfv1dh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="caption">If investors have less information about a company’s financial health, the uncertainty could make it more expensive for the company to raise capital.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/screen-showing-bitcoin-trading-chart-N__BnvQ_w18">Nick Chong on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A tsunami of opposition</h2>

<p>If a business wants to be a publicly traded company, it has to register with the SEC, which governs and regulates this process. Once registered, the company has to disclose its financial performance every three months, <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/07/2026-09095/semiannual-reporting">a requirement that has held since 1970</a>. </p>

<p>Whenever the agency issues a new rule, it opens it up to comments first, just like other government agencies do. That feedback is meant to shape the final rule before it becomes codified.</p>

<p>What’s unusual in this case is the overwhelming degree of opposition – more than 99% of all comments, many from retail and individual investors, according to my tracker.</p>

<p>“My husband worked for Enron. We lost most of our retirement savings when their fraudulent activity came to light,” <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-2576452.htm">wrote one commenter</a>. “We were still young enough to make some of that income back, but we knew many retirees who ended up working into their 80’s. Quarterly reporting is a gate keeper. Keep it.” </p>

<p><a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-2588027.htm">Wrote another</a>: “I rely on quarterly reporting for the same reason your child gets a quarterly report card. … There the metaphor ends, because a good teacher can catch failing performance and course correct with parents long before report cards are issued. Investors do not have that luxury.”</p>

<p>Some point out that the commission’s claim of company savings on compliance costs is overblown. The estimated average savings, according to the proposal, is <a href="https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11414.pdf">around US$200,000</a> a year per firm, which is a drop in the bucket for a typical public corporation. </p>

<p>But more broadly, the comments reveal how much this rule could matter to ordinary investors. Retirement savings, through accounts like 401(k) plans and individual retirement accounts, are directly exposed to company performance, whether or not the fund in question is diversified. That means any reduction in financial transparency has direct implications on how the investments of the funds are monitored. </p>

<p>That risk was laid out <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-944260-2915237.pdf">in a letter</a> from the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, or SIFMA. The trade group wrote that the estimated net savings “could be offset or outweighed by an increase in the cost of capital as investors demand higher risk premia for less timely information.”</p>

<p>Federated Hermes, an asset manager, <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-947359-2921191.pdf">also pointed</a> to this scenario: “Issuers that elect semiannual reporting may face signaling risks, as investors could interpret such a choice as reflecting reduced transparency,” the letter said. “This may affect analyst coverage and cost of capital.”</p>

<h2>Companies weigh in</h2>

<p>As for the companies themselves, it’s too early to say whether they would take advantage of the six-month option. But several have said they would choose to report less frequently. </p>

<p>Drugmaker Eli Lilly is one example, <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-943641-2913726.pdf">making clear its preference</a> in its official comment, while <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-923140-2837458.pdf">letters from Financial Executives International</a>, an industry lobby, stated that 58% of the member companies it surveyed suggested they would change.</p>

<p>For its part, the commission is still evaluating all the feedback before its leadership takes a vote. Traditionally, it’s led by five commissioners, with three representing the party in power and two from the opposition. However, in this case, the two Democratic seats in the minority are currently vacant, and one Republican seat is about <a href="https://www.plansponsor.com/hester-peirce-to-depart-as-sec-commissioner-on-october-2/">to be vacated</a>.</p>

<p>With so few votes on hand, the commission may in fact change its rules so that this proposal could clear with support from only two commissioners. On Sept. 30, 2026, it suggested a <a href="https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/final/2026/34-106537.pdf">rule change</a> so that the two votes would suffice.</p>

<p>For now, SEC Chair Paul Atkins seems undeterred and <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/sec-chair-defends-proposal-to-allow-companies-to-report-earnings-only-twice-a-year-203339554.html">has stated</a> that the commission is moving ahead. </p>

<p>How many companies will make the move given the concerns laid out in the comments, however, remains an open question. </p>

<p>As the SEC’s own Investor Advisory Committee, an independent body, <a href="https://www.sec.gov/comments/S7-2026-15/s7202615-913379-2799793.pdf">put it</a>: “The evidence does not support the view that short-termism is a major problem for U.S. public companies today, nor is there strong evidence to support the view that costs for public companies would be significantly reduced.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289338/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
